title: 1988–1994: Building Up Steam
tagline: S&L crisis · Gulf War · Collapse of the Soviet bloc · Clinton's economic plan · The dawn of the information superhighway

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: The deficits, S&L losses, and trade frictions left by Reaganomics came due in these seven years and were then steadily worked off. The third oil crisis and the S&L crisis triggered a mild recession in 1990 (NBER: Jul 1990 – Mar 1991), but from 1992 the US entered a steady, sustained expansion — the 'building up' phase of the long 1990s bull market.

The external environment changed dramatically: the Soviet bloc fell apart in 1989–1991, the Berlin Wall came down, and the Soviet Union dissolved; the Gulf War broke out in 1991; Japan's asset bubble burst. The end of the Cold War made the US the sole superpower and set the prologue for the global expansion of 'American capitalism' in the 1990s.

When Clinton took office in 1993, he placed fiscal discipline, free trade, and information technology at the center of his agenda. Commercial use of the internet took off in 1994 and the 'information superhighway' concept took shape. These seven years were, in effect, the foundation of the 1990s boom.

items.body: GDP grew 4.2% in 1988 and 3.7% in 1989, but the S&L industry — built on 1980s deregulation, moral hazard, and high rates — collapsed. In August 1989 Congress passed FIRREA (the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act), creating the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC) to wind down failed thrifts. The eventual rescue cost was roughly $124 billion, about 2% of GDP at the time.

Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990, and oil prices spiked from about $17 to about $40 (the third oil crisis). The US entered recession in Q3 1990 (NBER: Jul 1990 – Mar 1991). The Gulf War ran from January 17 to February 28, 1991, and oil prices fell back. The post-recession recovery was weak — 1991 GDP was −0.1% — as banks tightened credit and households and firms repaired their balance sheets against the backdrop of a large fiscal deficit. The Fed cut rates five times in 1991 to 3.5%, a near-30-year low.

Recovery firmed in 1992 with GDP at +3.5%. Clinton's 1993 economic plan combined deficit reduction, stable monetary policy, export promotion, and direct support for industrial technology. The federal deficit shrank for the first time in 1993. The 1994 economy was strong (GDP +4.0%), but inflation pressure prompted six Fed hikes (fed funds to 5.5%), making 1994 the 'bond market massacre' year.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: Finance Overtakes Manufacturing
body: In 1990, finance and real estate value added overtook manufacturing as a share of GDP for the first time. By 1994 the split was 18% finance and real estate versus 16% manufacturing — the manufacturing-led era was formally over. Wholesale and retail held steady at 13%.

Deindustrialization accelerated: manufacturing's share of total corporate profits fell from 28.9% in 1987 to 23.9% in 1994. Overseas profits' share fell from 22.0% to 18.2% as Japanese and European manufacturers pushed back against US multinationals. Services' share of profits more than doubled, from 3.9% to 8.5%.

Inside manufacturing, autos and other transportation equipment diverged for the first time: autos and parts saw annualized profit growth of +63% (Chrysler and Ford restructured after their crises), while other transportation equipment (aerospace, shipbuilding, rail) ran at −12.4% — a by-product of the structural shift from 'Cold War military' to 'civilian consumer'.
The US effective corporate tax rate fell from 34% in 1987 to 27% in 1991, rebounding to 29% in 1994 — the combined effect of Reagan-era cuts and modest Clinton-era hikes.

sections.heading: The Financial System: Resolving the S&L Crisis
body: 1980s 'deregulation plus federal deposit insurance' bred moral hazard in the thrift industry: investments shifted toward high-risk, high-return assets, with booming book values masking growing losses. In 1988 regulators spent $96 billion to close 185 thrifts; the crisis peaked in 1989.

FIRREA (August 9, 1989) abolished the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation (FSLIC), folding its functions into the FDIC; the OTS was created for supervision and the RTC for resolution. From 1989 to 1992 the RTC resolved over a thousand thrifts and disposed of roughly $400 billion in assets.

The 1991 FDIC Improvement Act (FDICIA) established the principle of 'prompt corrective action' (PCA) — an early prototype of the 'too big to fail' framework that would shape the 1990s philosophy of financial regulation.

items.body: On November 8, George H. W. Bush defeated Dukakis, extending Republican control eight years after Reagan.
items.title: Bush Sr. Elected

items.body: China's Tiananmen incident; Solidarity began governing in Poland in June; the Berlin Wall fell on November 9. The Cold War order began to crumble.
items.title: Tiananmen and the Start of the Soviet Bloc's Collapse

items.body: FIRREA was signed, setting up the RTC to resolve failed thrifts.
items.title: FIRREA Signed

items.body: The Cold War order disintegrated further.
items.title: German Reunification

items.body: On August 6, Tim Berners-Lee published the first website — the birth of the World Wide Web.
items.title: Internet Commercialization Milestone

items.body: Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet Union formally dissolved. The Cold War ended.
items.title: Soviet Union Dissolves

items.body: On November 3, Clinton defeated Bush; the Democrats returned to the White House after twelve years.
items.title: Clinton Elected

items.body: Clinton's modest tax hikes and spending cuts opened an era of fiscal discipline.
items.title: Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993

items.body: The House passed NAFTA in November; it took effect on January 1, 1994.
items.title: NAFTA Passed

items.body: Same day: the Zapatista uprising in Mexico.
items.title: NAFTA Takes Effect and the Zapatista Uprising

items.body: Netscape Communications was founded in April (Netscape Navigator shipped in October); MIT established the W3C.
items.title: Netscape Founded and W3C Established

items.body: December 20: the Mexican peso devalued, triggering a Latin American financial crisis.
